title: Training Designer: Gas terminal release and fire, 2020
audience: Training managers, instructors and competence assessors
status: Learning purposes: not a statutory document. Derived from a ProbeMatrix investigation export; learnings are evidence-linked but should be validated by the organisation before adoption. Draft learnings: the investigation status is in progress.

incident.title: Hazira gas terminal condensate release and fire

data_quality.text: Draft learnings from an unreviewed analysis: the export's investigation status is in progress and no finding is marked as edited by a person. Validate every item before adoption.

bottom_line.text: Real competence gaps: specifying and testing pressure parts, recording calibration changes, and switching from locating a leak to isolating it.
Most of what went wrong is a system problem training cannot fix: no specification, no return-to-service procedure, no remote isolation, no isolation authority in the plan.
Control-room staff held emergency duties after a four-day general course with no defined qualification or simulator practice; a qualification standard is needed before more courses.
Teach to the level of the cause: crew modules for acts and conditions, supervisor and manager modules for checks, warnings and authority.

rows: Recognising a seal that does not match the original, and stopping to ask for the specification
Having a specification and an approved substitute to fit
Testing a pressure joint to the written test pressure before return to service
A return-to-service procedure that sets the test, the test pressure and the witness
Technical support for specification and verification decisions
Recording every calibration setting change, with as-found and as-left values
A checklist for critical high-pressure calibration jobs
Switching from locating the leak to isolating from a distance when access is denied
A defined qualification and simulator practice before emergency duty
Written isolation criteria and delegated authority in the emergency plan
Reporting a release to the control room that can act, in standard words
A direct line from security posts to each process control room
Characterising damage to hazardous-area equipment item by item
A preventive inspection programme for flameproof equipment
Recognising a not-in-kind replacement as a change that needs review
Plant-specific audit checklists that need evidence for each compliance claim

items.title: Returning pressure equipment to service
items.objective: Given a pressure-boundary job, the learner names the part specification, the test, the test pressure and the witness, and stops the job when any of them is missing.
content: Case: a meter in service since 1986 was built for a rectangular-slot gasket; its specification was lost, and locally bought O-rings were fitted as regular practice with no specification or quality check.
Case: after the last seal change the system was only brought to operating pressure; there was no hydro test to design pressure, and the meter was in use when it failed.
Activity: sort sample seals into "matches the specification", "approved substitute" and "stop and ask", using the item's records.
Activity: walk a return-to-service record and find what is missing.
System note: this module works only with a written specification and a return-to-service procedure; where they are missing, the learner is taught to stop and ask, not to fill the gap.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Practical: complete a return-to-service record for a simulated job, observed by an assessor.
Questions: assessment items on specification and testing.

items.title: Responding to a release you cannot reach
items.objective: In a simulated release that denies access, the learner reports "access denied", names the isolation points that can be reached safely and asks for the isolation decision without delay.
items.audience: Control-room engineers and operators, security staff
items.duration: Half a day, simulator or tabletop
content: Case: security staff saw the cloud first; the control room heard of it as "some vapour cloud or steam leakage"; engineers tried to approach and were driven back; the first valve was closed by hand at 03:01.
Case: the gas detectors only lit a panel and started no protective action.
Activity: on the area drawing, mark which valves isolate each section and where each is worked from.
Activity: practise the standard release message between a security post and the control room.
System note: this module supports, and does not replace, remote isolation, executive gas detection and written isolation authority, which are system changes for manager-coach.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Simulator or tabletop scenario, scored on the time to the isolation request and the content of the release message.
Questions: assessment items on alarms and isolation.

items.title: Calibration records that show what was done
items.objective: The learner records every setting changed during a calibration, including changes reversed, with as-found and as-left values, and does not sign a record that leaves a change out.
content: Case: during a calibration in December 2019 the meter's range setting was changed and later changed back, with neither change on the signed records and no checklist.
Activity: complete a calibration record from a worked example that includes a reversed change.
System note: a calibration checklist for critical meters is a system change; until it exists, the learner uses the worked example as the record.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Practical: an assessor reviews a completed calibration record for a critical meter.

items.title: Accepting work back: hold points, notifications and permits
items.objective: The supervisor applies the return-to-service hold points: a recorded test with a witness, the part's specification reference, a closed notification and a closed permit, and declines to accept work that lacks them.
content: Case: the seal job ran on a maintenance notification with no job safety analysis; no one checked the part, the method or the test, and the notification was not closed or reviewed.
Activity: coaching conversation on a job handed back late in the shift without a test record.
Activity: map each hold point to the form where it should live (permit, return-to-service certificate, shift log or job card).
System note: supervisors can hold the line only if the work-order system and management back them; those changes are for manager-coach.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Observed coaching conversation, assessed against the hold points.
Questions: assessment items on supervision and the levels of cause.

items.title: Reading repeat failures and integrity warnings
items.objective: The manager recognises a repeat failure or an unactioned inspection result as a reliability warning and routes it to a root-cause review or a fitness-for-service decision.
content: Case: the same meter's gasket was replaced three times in about 22 months with the same substitute part, and none of the repairs triggered a root-cause review.
Case: pipe-wall loss found in 2017 had no corrective plan three years later, and pitting found in July 2019 on a zero-corrosion-allowance line was treated by painting.
Activity: from a maintenance history extract, find the bad actors and decide the route for each.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Case review: the manager presents the route chosen for each warning and why.

items.title: Isolation authority and the emergency plan
items.objective: The senior shift leader states the isolation criteria, the valves and the delegated authority for each release scenario, and leads an isolation decision in a night-shift exercise without waiting for escalation.
content: Case: the plan named the hydrocarbon-leak scenario but not isolation; no one below the plant manager held standing authority to close the emergency valves; escalation ran one call at a time.
Activity: tabletop exercise with injects from the night, run without senior staff present.
System note: the criteria and authority must first be written into the plan by its owner; until then this module surfaces the gap rather than teaching an authority that does not exist.
Competence standard: to be set by the competence system owner
Refresher interval: to be set by the competence system owner
assessment: Tabletop exercise, assessed on the time to the isolation decision and the use of the criteria.

items.situation: Decision point 1: the original seal is not in stores and the meter is needed back. Decision point 2: the job is finished and nobody has written down a test pressure. Decision point 3: operations ask to put the meter back on line now.
prompts: Facilitator note: let the group say what made the usual O-ring the sensible choice at the time before discussing alternatives.
Facilitator note: ask what needs to exist (a specification, a procedure, a named witness) for "stop" to be the easy answer.
Facilitator note: close on what the learner will ask for on the next job, not on blame.

items.situation: Decision point 1: a call reports "some vapour cloud" and the gas alarm sounds. Decision point 2: you go out and cannot see or approach the source. Decision point 3: the person who can authorise isolation is not on site.
prompts: Facilitator note: pause at each decision point and ask what the learner knows at that moment, not what the investigation later found.
Facilitator note: draw out which valves could be reached safely and who could be asked.
Facilitator note: record the system changes the group names for the manager-coach list.

items.situation: Decision point 1: mid-calibration, a range setting has to be changed to complete a check. Decision point 2: the setting is put back. Decision point 3: the record is handed over for signature.
prompts: Facilitator note: ask where the reversed change would be recorded today.
Facilitator note: ask who would notice if it were not recorded, and when.

items.question: The seal in stores does not match the shape of the groove, and nobody can find the specification. What do you do?
items.why: Recognising a non-specified pressure part and stopping.
items.answer: Stop and ask the supervisor for the specification or an approved substitute; do not fit the part on the strength of "what we normally use".
items.good_evidence: The learner names who they would ask and where the specification should be recorded.

items.question: Why does pressurising a repaired joint to operating pressure not prove it?
items.why: Understanding the purpose of a test to design pressure.
items.answer: Operating pressure does not prove the joint against the pressures it must withstand; a written test to the test pressure, with a witness, is what proves it.
items.good_evidence: The learner names the test, the test pressure source and the witness.

items.question: What three things must be on the record before pressure-boundary equipment returns to service?
items.answer: The part's specification reference, a recorded test to the written test pressure, and the witness's signature.

items.question: You are about to replace the same gasket on the same meter for the third time. What should happen besides the repair?
items.why: Recognising a repeat failure as a reliability warning.
items.answer: Record it as a repeat failure and raise a root-cause request, so the item is reviewed rather than repaired again unseen.
items.good_evidence: The learner names where the repeat is recorded and who receives the request.

items.question: During calibration you change a range setting and later change it back. What goes on the record?
items.answer: Both changes, with as-found and as-left values; the signed record must show what was done, not only the end state.
items.good_evidence: A completed example record that includes the reversed change.

items.question: On this site, what did a gas alarm on the annunciator panel do by itself?
items.why: Knowing what the alarm does and does not do.
items.answer: It only displayed the alarm; it did not shut down the plant or start fire suppression, so every protective action depended on people.
items.good_evidence: The learner can say which alarms on their unit trip equipment and which do not.

items.question: You go out to find a leak and the cloud stops you approaching. What is your next step?
items.answer: Stop approaching, tell the control room "access denied", and ask for isolation from the points that can be reached safely.
items.good_evidence: The learner names the isolation points for their area and where they are worked from.

items.question: You are on a security post and see a white cloud near a process area. Whom do you call first, and what do you say?
items.why: Reporting a release so the control room can act.
items.answer: The control room for that area, saying "hydrocarbon release", where it is and how big it is.
items.good_evidence: The learner names the right control room for each area they watch.

items.question: A flameproof lamp still lights, but three bolts are missing from its cover. Is it still flameproof?
items.why: Recognising a defect in explosion-protected equipment.
items.answer: No. A flameproof fitting with missing bolts or an open cover is not flameproof; report it and have it made safe the same shift.
items.good_evidence: The learner lists what to check on a flameproof fitting on rounds.

items.question: Level of cause: "Locally bought O-rings were fitted as regular practice because the original specification had been lost and no one owned re-establishing it." At which level does the main fix sit, and why?
items.why: Placing a cause at its level (L1 to L4).
items.answer: Level 4, organisational: the missing specification and owner are resource and policy conditions. The fix is an owner and a specification, not an instruction to the fitter.
items.good_evidence: The learner separates the act (L1) from the organisational condition (L4).

items.question: Level of cause: "The maintenance notification was not closed or reviewed after the job." Which level is this, and what kind of fix does it need?
items.why: Placing a cause at its level (L1 to L4).
items.answer: Level 3, supervision: a check and correction that did not happen. The fix is a change to checks and oversight, such as a close-out review, not a reminder to the crew.
items.good_evidence: The learner names a supervision-level fix.

items.question: Level of cause: "The vapour cloud stopped people approaching the isolation valves." Which level is this?
items.why: Placing a cause at its level (L1 to L4).
items.answer: Level 2, preconditions: the physical and technological environment at the time. It explains why the act of isolating was delayed, and points to a design change (remote operation).
items.good_evidence: The learner links the precondition to an engineering fix.

items.question: Why is more training alone not enough to close the control-room competence gap seen here?
items.answer: There was no defined qualification and no simulator practice, and the valves and alarms needed people to act. Training supports, but does not replace, a qualification standard used for rostering and the engineering changes.
items.good_evidence: The learner names one system change that must accompany the training.

Shift in-charges, control-room staff and security staff

Detection-to-notification and detection-to-isolation times in drills, against the site's time standard
